title: Cold War Choir Practice by Ro Reddick at MCC #coldwarchoirpractice #m...
transcript: There's no world in which the Cold War would ever inspire me to write a play. And yet, someone has done it marvelously and it's a must-see. In Ro Reddick's wildly original and strange new play, a ten year old girl, her father, and her grandmother are living in Syracuse above the roller rink that they own. With the backdrop of Reagan-era patriotism, she and the rest of the Seedlings of Peace Children's Chorus try to fend off nuclear war through song. When her politician uncle visits over the holidays with his alarmingly parched wife, family drama and suspicious activity unfold. It's a lot to unpack, and the genius of this piece can't be fully captured in a quick video review. I'll just say that I was really struck by how satisfyingly entertaining and funny this play is without sacrificing any complexity. It's dense, with each character and relationship clearly revealing or representing something that's otherwise kind of slippery to articulate. It's a remarkable collision of big ideas such as conformity, paranoia, and consumerism, with the lives of an everyday family. Specifically putting the story through the lens of a young Black girl adds an additional layer of poignance, illustrating this desire for both control and hope in an unkind world, or even just an acknowledgement from the forces and groups that govern all of us but tend to have selective attention. All that said, this play couldn't be more relevant and I cannot recommend it enough. Cold War Choir Practice is running at MCC through the end of March. With that, another program for my collection.
